records.source: Μετὰ ταῦτα χωρισθεὶς ἐκ τῶν Ἀθηνῶν ἦλθεν εἰς Κόρινθον.
records.gloss: After these things having departed from the Athens he came to Corinth.
pieces: After this, Paul left Athens and went on to Corinth.

L.1: After these things, having left Athens, he came to Corinth.

R.1: After this, Paul left the city of Athens and went to the city of Corinth.

decisions.choice: Corinth: the leading city of the province of Achaia
decisions.reason: Corinth stood on the narrow neck of land between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese, with a port on each sea (Cenchreae, 18:18, was the eastern one). Rome destroyed the old city in 146 BC, and Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony in 44 BC. It was the seat of the proconsul of Achaia (18:12).

decisions.choice: he: Paul, who had been in Athens (17:16-34)
decisions.reason: Paul was alone in Athens; Silas and Timothy join him later (18:5).

decisions.choice: Paul
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Paul at the start of a new chapter and a new place.

records.heading: Paul comes to Corinth

records.source: καὶ εὑρών τινα Ἰουδαῖον ὀνόματι Ἀκύλαν, Ποντικὸν τῷ γένει, προσφάτως ἐληλυθότα ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰταλίας καὶ Πρίσκιλλαν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ διὰ τὸ διατεταχέναι Κλαύδιον χωρίζεσθαι πάντας τοὺς Ἰουδαίους ἀπὸ τῆς Ῥώμης, προσῆλθεν αὐτοῖς, καὶ διὰ τὸ ὁμότεχνον εἶναι ἔμενεν παρ’ αὐτοῖς καὶ ἠργάζετο, ἦσαν γὰρ σκηνοποιοὶ τῇ τέχνῃ.
records.gloss: And having found a certain Jew by name Aquila, of Pontus by the birth, recently having come from the Italy, and Priscilla wife of him, because of the having commanded Claudius to depart all the Jews from the Rome, he came to them, \v 3 and because of the same trade to be he stayed with them and worked; they were for tentmakers by the trade.
pieces: There he met a Jew called Aquila, born in Pontus, who had lately arrived from Italy with his wife Priscilla, since Claudius had ordered every Jew to leave Rome. Paul went to see them,
and because he and they worked at the same craft, he stayed in their home and worked with them. By trade they were tentmakers.

L.2: And having found a certain Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy, and Priscilla his wife, because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome, he went to them,
L.3: and because he was of the same trade, he stayed with them and worked; for they were tentmakers by trade.

R.2: In Corinth Paul met a Jew named Aquila. He came from Pontus, but he and his wife Priscilla had recently come to Corinth from Italy. They left Italy because the emperor Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave the city of Rome. Paul went to visit them.
R.3: They did the same kind of work as Paul: they made tents. So Paul stayed with them and worked with them.

decisions.choice: Claudius's order sending the Jews out of Rome, probably about AD 49
alternatives: a date early in Claudius's reign, AD 41
decisions.reason: Claudius was emperor from AD 41 to 54. The Roman writer Suetonius (Claudius 25.4) says that Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because they were constantly rioting at the prompting of "Chrestus", a form of the name Christ. The date AD 49 comes from the fifth-century writer Orosius, whose source is not known. Dio Cassius (60.6.6) speaks instead of a ban on Jewish meetings in AD 41, which some connect with the same events. So the year is not certain.

decisions.choice: all the Jews: the order as it was given, not a claim that every Jew left
alternatives: every Jew without exception left Rome
decisions.reason: Luke reports the terms of the order. Jews were living in Rome again a few years later: Priscilla and Aquila themselves were back there when Paul wrote Romans (Romans 16:3), and Paul meets the Jewish leaders of Rome in 28:17.

decisions.choice: Aquila and Priscilla: a Jewish couple from Pontus who had lived in Rome
alternatives: already leaders of the church in Rome
decisions.reason: Pontus was a region on the south coast of the Black Sea. The couple appear again in 18:18, 18:26, Romans 16:3, 1 Corinthians 16:19 and 2 Timothy 4:19, where Paul calls her Prisca, the shorter form of the name. Luke does not say whether they were already believers when Paul met them.

decisions.choice: tentmakers: people who made tents, perhaps leatherworkers more generally
decisions.reason: The word means a maker of tents. Tents were made of leather or of cloth woven from goat hair, so the trade may have been leatherwork of many kinds. The word itself does not settle which material they worked in.

decisions.choice: Paul worked with his hands to support himself
alternatives: he worked only to help the couple
decisions.reason: Paul says he earned his own living so as not to be a burden to the churches (20:34; 1 Corinthians 4:12; 9:6-15; 1 Thessalonians 2:9).

decisions.choice: the Greek order, close to other literal versions
decisions.reason: Literal follows the Greek sentence closely, so it will look like other word-for-word translations here.

decisions.choice: the emperor Claudius
decisions.reason: Readable says who Claudius was.

records.source: διελέγετο δὲ ἐν τῇ συναγωγῇ κατὰ πᾶν σάββατον, ἔπειθέν τε Ἰουδαίους καὶ Ἕλληνας.
records.gloss: He was reasoning now in the synagogue on every Sabbath, persuading both Jews and Greeks.
pieces: Each Sabbath he debated in the synagogue, seeking to win over Jews and Greeks alike.

L.4: And he was reasoning in the synagogue every Sabbath and was persuading both Jews and Greeks.

R.4: Every Sabbath day Paul went to the synagogue. He talked with the people there and tried to convince both Jews and Greeks to believe the message about Jesus.

decisions.choice: reasoning: discussing and arguing, from the Scriptures
alternatives: giving a speech with no exchange
decisions.reason: The verb is used of Paul's dialogues in the synagogues (17:2, 17:17, 18:19, 19:8). In 17:2-3 he reasons from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise.

decisions.choice: was persuading: he kept trying to persuade
decisions.reason: The tense describes an action that went on. It can mean either that he tried to persuade or that he won people over; 18:8 shows that some did believe.

decisions.choice: Greeks: Gentiles who attended the synagogue
decisions.reason: Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God often came to synagogues (13:16, 13:26, 17:4). Titius Justus in 18:7 is one of them.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: no addition
alternatives: Codex Bezae adds that he put in the name of the Lord Jesus
decisions.reason: Codex Bezae and some other witnesses of the Western text expand the verse, saying that Paul inserted the name of the Lord Jesus as he spoke. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: to believe the message about Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable says what Paul wanted them to be persuaded of, as 18:5 states.

records.source: Ὡς δὲ κατῆλθον ἀπὸ τῆς Μακεδονίας ὅ τε Σιλᾶς καὶ ὁ Τιμόθεος, συνείχετο τῷ λόγῳ ὁ Παῦλος, διαμαρτυρόμενος τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις εἶναι τὸν χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν.
records.gloss: When now came down from the Macedonia both Silas and the Timothy, was being occupied with the word the Paul, earnestly testifying to the Jews to be the Christ Jesus.
pieces: Once Silas and Timothy had come down from Macedonia, Paul gave himself fully to the word, bearing witness to the Jews that Jesus is the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

L.5: And when both Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul was wholly occupied with the word, solemnly testifying to the Jews that the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} was Jesus.

R.5: Later Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia to join Paul. After that, Paul spent all his time telling people God's message. He told the Jews clearly that Jesus is the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, the one God had promised to send.

decisions.choice: Silas and Timothy rejoin Paul
alternatives: they meet him for the first time
decisions.reason: Paul had left them in Berea (17:14-15) and asked them to come to him quickly. 1 Thessalonians 3:6 says Timothy brought Paul good news from Thessalonica; Paul wrote that letter with Silvanus (Silas) and Timothy (1 Thessalonians 1:1).

decisions.choice: was wholly occupied with the word: he gave all his time to preaching
alternatives: he was pressed hard by the message
he was distressed about the message
decisions.reason: The verb means to be held fast or absorbed by something. Here it is likely that Paul could now stop his tentmaking for a time, perhaps because the friends from Macedonia brought gifts (2 Corinthians 11:9; Philippians 4:15).

decisions.choice: the Christ was Jesus: the promised Messiah is this man Jesus
alternatives: Jesus was a Christ, one anointed figure among others
decisions.reason: The word with the article is the subject: the one the Jews were waiting for is Jesus. It is a title here, not a second name. The same words come in 18:28 (compare 9:22, 17:3).

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "with the word"
alternatives: many later manuscripts read "in the spirit"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version ("pressed in the spirit"), have "in the spirit" in place of "with the word". The earliest manuscripts have "the word". Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: that Jesus is the Messiah (with Christ as the setting)
decisions.reason: Both orders say the same thing in English. Literal keeps the Greek order; Balanced and Readable use the order English readers expect.

decisions.choice: the one God had promised to send
decisions.reason: Readable explains the title.

records.heading: A year and a half in Corinth

records.source: ἀντιτασσομένων δὲ αὐτῶν καὶ βλασφημούντων ἐκτιναξάμενος τὰ ἱμάτια εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτούς· Τὸ αἷμα ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν ὑμῶν· καθαρὸς ἐγώ· ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν εἰς τὰ ἔθνη πορεύσομαι.
records.gloss: Opposing however of them and reviling, having shaken out the garments he said to them, The blood of you upon the head of you; clean I; from the now to the Gentiles I will go.
pieces: But they set themselves against him and spoke abusively, so he shook out his clothes and said to them, "Your blood is on your own heads. I am clear of it. From now on I am going to the Gentiles."

L.6: But when they opposed and reviled [him], he shook out [his] garments and said to them, "Your blood [be] on your head; I [am] clean. From now on I will go to the Gentiles."

R.6: But the Jews there argued against Paul and said insulting things. So Paul shook out his clothes, to show that he was no longer responsible for them. He said, "If God punishes you, the blame is yours, not mine. I have done what I should. From now on I will go to the Gentiles, the people who are not Jews."

decisions.choice: reviling: speaking abusively, of Paul and of the Jesus he preached
decisions.reason: The verb means to speak insults. Against people it is abuse; against God or Jesus it is blasphemy. Paul's message was about Jesus, so the insults probably touched both.

decisions.choice: shaking out his garments: a sign that he was done with them and not to blame
alternatives: brushing off dust after a journey
decisions.reason: A public gesture of breaking off. Nehemiah shook out his garment as a sign that God would shake out anyone who broke the oath (Nehemiah 5:13). Paul and Barnabas shook the dust off their feet at Pisidian Antioch (13:51), as Jesus had told his disciples to do (Luke 9:5).

decisions.choice: your blood on your head: you are responsible for your own fate, and I am free of blame
alternatives: a curse that they would die
decisions.reason: The words echo Ezekiel 33:4-9: a watchman who warns the people is free of guilt for those who do not listen. Compare 2 Samuel 1:16 and 20:26, where Paul says he is "clean from the blood" of all.

decisions.choice: to the Gentiles: here in Corinth he turns to the Gentiles
alternatives: he will never again preach to Jews
decisions.reason: Paul says the same in 13:46 and 28:28. In the next city he again goes first to the synagogue (18:19), so this is about the Jews of Corinth, not the Jews everywhere.

decisions.choice: to show that he was no longer responsible for them; If God punishes you, the blame is yours, not mine
alternatives: he shook out his clothes; your blood be on your head
decisions.reason: Readable explains the gesture and the saying, following the meaning notes.

decisions.choice: the Gentiles, the people who are not Jews
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word Gentiles.

records.source: καὶ μεταβὰς ἐκεῖθεν εἰσῆλθεν εἰς οἰκίαν τινὸς ὀνόματι Τιτίου Ἰούστου σεβομένου τὸν θεόν, οὗ ἡ οἰκία ἦν συνομοροῦσα τῇ συναγωγῇ.
records.gloss: And having departed from there he went into [the] house of a certain [one] by name Titius Justus, worshiping the God, of whom the house was adjoining the synagogue.
pieces: Paul left them and went over to the home of a man named Titius Justus, who worshiped God. His house stood right beside the synagogue.

L.7: And departing from there, he went into the house of a certain [man] named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.

R.7: Paul left the synagogue and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus. Titius Justus was not a Jew, but he worshiped God. His house was next to the synagogue.

decisions.choice: he went into the house: he began to teach there, not in the synagogue
alternatives: he moved his lodging from Aquila and Priscilla to Titius Justus
decisions.reason: "From there" points back to the synagogue of 18:4-6. The house became the place where Paul taught. Luke does not say that Paul stopped living with Aquila and Priscilla.

decisions.choice: a worshiper of God: a Gentile who worshiped Israel's God without becoming a Jew
decisions.reason: Luke uses this phrase for Gentiles who attended the synagogue, such as Lydia (16:14) and the Greeks in 17:4. Titius Justus is a Roman name.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "Titius Justus"
decisions.reason: The manuscripts differ over the name. Some have "Titus Justus", and many later ones, followed by the King James Version, have "Justus" alone. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Titius Justus was not a Jew, but he worshiped God
decisions.reason: Readable says what the phrase meant for a Gentile, following the meaning note. Luke does not say outright that he was a Gentile.

records.source: Κρίσπος δὲ ὁ ἀρχισυνάγωγος ἐπίστευσεν τῷ κυρίῳ σὺν ὅλῳ τῷ οἴκῳ αὐτοῦ, καὶ πολλοὶ τῶν Κορινθίων ἀκούοντες ἐπίστευον καὶ ἐβαπτίζοντο.
records.gloss: Crispus now the synagogue ruler believed in the Lord with whole the household of him, and many of the Corinthians hearing were believing and were being baptized.
pieces: Crispus, who led the synagogue, believed in the Lord, and so did everyone in his household. Many other people in Corinth heard the message, believed and were baptized.

L.8: And Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with his whole household, and many of the Corinthians, hearing, believed and were baptized.

R.8: Crispus was the leader of the synagogue. He and everyone in his house believed in the Lord. Many other people in Corinth heard the message about Jesus. They believed in Jesus and were baptized.

decisions.choice: Crispus, the synagogue ruler: the official who arranged the synagogue's meetings
decisions.reason: The ruler of a synagogue chose who would read and speak (13:15; Luke 8:41). Paul says he baptized Crispus himself (1 Corinthians 1:14). His coming to faith was a striking event after 18:6.

decisions.choice: his whole household: his family and everyone who lived in his house
decisions.reason: A household included family members, slaves and others who lived there, as with Cornelius (10:2, 11:14) and the jailer at Philippi (16:31-34).

decisions.choice: were believing and were being baptized: one after another, over a period of time
decisions.reason: The tenses describe something that kept happening during Paul's stay (18:11).

decisions.choice: the Lord: Jesus
decisions.reason: Paul's message was about Jesus (18:5), and "believed in the Lord" in Acts usually means believing in Jesus (9:42, 11:17, 16:31).

decisions.choice: heard the message (B); heard the message about Jesus (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what was heard.

records.source: εἶπεν δὲ ὁ κύριος ἐν νυκτὶ δι’ ὁράματος τῷ Παύλῳ· Μὴ φοβοῦ, ἀλλὰ λάλει καὶ μὴ σιωπήσῃς, διότι ἐγώ εἰμι μετὰ σοῦ καὶ οὐδεὶς ἐπιθήσεταί σοι τοῦ κακῶσαί σε, διότι λαός ἐστί μοι πολὺς ἐν τῇ πόλει ταύτῃ.
records.gloss: Said now the Lord in night through a vision to the Paul, Not fear, but speak and not be silent, \v 10 because I am with you and no one will set upon you to harm you, because people is to me much in the city this.
pieces: In a vision at night the Lord told Paul, "Stop being afraid. Go on speaking, and do not fall silent.
I am with you. No one will lay a hand on you to hurt you, because many in this city belong to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

L.9: And the Lord said to Paul in [the] night through a vision, "Do not fear, but speak and do not be silent,
L.10: because I am with you, and no one will set upon you to harm you, because there are many people [belonging] to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} in this city."

R.9: One night Paul saw a vision. In it the Lord said to him, "Do not be afraid. Keep telling people about {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and do not stop.
R.10: I am with you. No one will attack you or hurt you. There are many people in this city who belong to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

decisions.choice: the Lord: the risen Jesus
decisions.reason: Paul sees and hears the risen Jesus in other visions (9:4-6, 22:17-21, 23:11). In 23:11 the Lord who stands by him at night tells him to take heart, as here.

decisions.choice: stop being afraid; keep on speaking
alternatives: do not start to be afraid
decisions.reason: The commands are in the present tense, which suits going on with something or stopping something already under way. Paul was speaking under threat (18:6), and 1 Corinthians 2:3 says he was with them "in weakness and in fear and in much trembling".

decisions.choice: I am with you: the promise God gives to those he sends
decisions.reason: God says these words to Jacob (Genesis 28:15), to Joshua (Joshua 1:5, 1:9) and to Jeremiah, adding "do not be afraid" (Jeremiah 1:8; compare Isaiah 41:10). Jesus promised the same to his disciples (Matthew 28:20).

decisions.choice: set upon you to harm you: attack you so as to do you harm
decisions.reason: Paul is still accused (18:12), but no one is able to hurt him.

decisions.choice: many people belonging to me: many in Corinth whom the Lord will bring to faith
decisions.reason: The word for people is the one used for Israel as God's people. In 15:14 James says God has taken from the Gentiles "a people for his name". Here the Lord counts as his own many in Corinth who have not yet believed.

decisions.choice: keep telling people about me
decisions.reason: Readable says what Paul was to speak about.

records.source: ἐκάθισεν δὲ ἐνιαυτὸν καὶ μῆνας ἓξ διδάσκων ἐν αὐτοῖς τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ.
records.gloss: He sat now a year and months six teaching among them the word of the God.
pieces: Paul stayed on for eighteen months, teaching the word of God among them.

L.11: And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.

R.11: Paul stayed in Corinth for a year and a half. He taught the people there the word of God.

decisions.choice: sat: stayed, settled
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to sit or to settle in a place. Here it says how long Paul stayed.

decisions.choice: a year and six months: perhaps the length of the whole stay, or the time before the events of 18:12
decisions.reason: After the hearing before Gallio, Paul stays "many days more" (18:18). It is not clear whether those days are counted in the eighteen months.

records.source: Γαλλίωνος δὲ ἀνθυπάτου ὄντος τῆς Ἀχαΐας κατεπέστησαν ὁμοθυμαδὸν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι τῷ Παύλῳ καὶ ἤγαγον αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τὸ βῆμα, λέγοντες ὅτι Παρὰ τὸν νόμον ἀναπείθει οὗτος τοὺς ἀνθρώπους σέβεσθαι τὸν θεόν.
records.gloss: Gallio however proconsul being of the Achaia, rose up with one accord the Jews against the Paul and led him to the judgment seat, \v 13 saying that, Contrary to the law persuades this [one] the men to worship the God.
pieces: But while Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews joined forces against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat.
Their charge was this: "He is talking people into worshiping God in a way the law does not allow."

L.12: But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews with one accord rose up against Paul and led him to the judgment seat,
L.13: saying, "This [man] persuades {{gender:people|men}} to worship God contrary to the law."

R.12: Later, Gallio became proconsul, the Roman governor of Achaia. Then the Jews all joined together against Paul and took him to court in front of Gallio.
R.13: They said, "This man is teaching people to worship God in a way that breaks the law."

decisions.choice: Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, about AD 51-52
decisions.reason: Gallio was the brother of the philosopher Seneca. A letter of the emperor Claudius carved in stone at Delphi (the Gallio inscription) names him as proconsul. It dates his year in office to about AD 51-52, which helps date Paul's stay in Corinth. A proconsul governed a senatorial province such as Achaia, usually for one year.

decisions.choice: when Gallio was proconsul: perhaps soon after he arrived
alternatives: at the end of his term
decisions.reason: The phrase sets the time. A new governor was a natural moment for the Jews to try their case again, but Luke does not say so.

decisions.choice: the judgment seat: the raised platform where the governor heard cases
decisions.reason: The word means a raised step or platform. Roman officials sat on it in a public place to give judgment (25:6, 25:10, 25:17; Matthew 27:19).

decisions.choice: the law: Jewish law, or Roman law
decisions.reason: The accusers may have meant that Paul's teaching broke Roman law, which allowed Judaism but not new cults. Gallio takes it as a matter of the Jews' own law (18:15). The word alone does not say which law is meant.

decisions.choice: men: people, men and women
decisions.reason: The charge is about anyone Paul persuades, and women were among the believers (17:4, 17:12, 18:2).

decisions.choice: people
decisions.reason: The word means people here; Literal has a gender span.

decisions.choice: proconsul, the Roman governor; took him to court in front of Gallio
alternatives: proconsul; led him to the judgment seat
decisions.reason: Readable explains the title and what the judgment seat was.

records.source: μέλλοντος δὲ τοῦ Παύλου ἀνοίγειν τὸ στόμα εἶπεν ὁ Γαλλίων πρὸς τοὺς Ἰουδαίους· Εἰ μὲν ἦν ἀδίκημά τι ἢ ῥᾳδιούργημα πονηρόν, ὦ Ἰουδαῖοι, κατὰ λόγον ἂν ἀνεσχόμην ὑμῶν·
records.gloss: Being about now the Paul to open the mouth, said the Gallio to the Jews, If indeed it was wrongdoing some or crime wicked, O Jews, according to reason I would have borne with you;
pieces: Paul was about to speak when Gallio said to the Jews, "If this were some wrong or a serious crime, you Jews, I would have good reason to take up your case.

L.14: But when Paul was about to open [his] mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, "If indeed it were some wrongdoing or wicked crime, O Jews, I would reasonably have put up with you;

R.14: Paul was ready to answer, but Gallio spoke first. He said to the Jews, "If this man had done something wrong or had committed a serious crime, I would of course listen to your complaint.

decisions.choice: to open his mouth: to begin his defense
decisions.reason: A common way of saying someone begins to speak (8:35, 10:34).

decisions.choice: wrongdoing or wicked crime: an offense against the law, or a serious act of fraud or villainy
decisions.reason: The first word means a legal wrong. The second means a reckless or wicked deed. Gallio means matters a Roman court would judge.

decisions.choice: if it were ... I would have: but it is not such a case
decisions.reason: The form of the sentence assumes the opposite is true: there is no crime here.

decisions.choice: I would reasonably have put up with you: it would be right for me to hear your case
alternatives: I would have been patient with your manners
decisions.reason: "Put up with" means to hear someone out. "According to reason" means as is fitting or right.

decisions.choice: a full stop, with the quotation still open
decisions.reason: The Greek sentence goes on into 18:15. Balanced and Readable end the English sentence here.

records.source: εἰ δὲ ζητήματά ἐστιν περὶ λόγου καὶ ὀνομάτων καὶ νόμου τοῦ καθ’ ὑμᾶς, ὄψεσθε αὐτοί· κριτὴς ἐγὼ τούτων οὐ βούλομαι εἶναι.
records.gloss: if however questions it is about word and names and law of the according to you, you will see [to it] yourselves; a judge I of these things not wish to be.
pieces: But these are disputes over teaching and titles and your own law. Deal with them yourselves. I will not sit in judgment on matters like these."

L.15: but if it is questions about a word and names and your own law, you will see [to it] yourselves; I do not wish to be a judge of these things."

R.15: But you are arguing about words and names and your own Jewish law. You must settle that yourselves. I will not be a judge of things like that."

decisions.choice: but if: but since, as is the case
decisions.reason: After the unreal condition in 18:14, this condition states what Gallio thinks the matter really is.

decisions.choice: a word and names: arguments about teaching and about names or titles
decisions.reason: Gallio speaks with contempt of Jewish disputes. The "names" may be whether Jesus is the Messiah (18:5): the claim was about a name and a title.

decisions.choice: you will see to it yourselves: deal with it yourselves
alternatives: a prediction that they will see
decisions.reason: A future used as a command, as in Matthew 27:4, 27:24.

decisions.choice: Gallio refuses to try the case
alternatives: he finds Paul innocent of a crime
decisions.reason: He treats the dispute as a matter inside Judaism. In practice this left Paul free to go on preaching in Corinth.

decisions.choice: teaching and titles
decisions.reason: Balanced says what kind of words and names were argued over, following the meaning note.

records.source: καὶ ἀπήλασεν αὐτοὺς ἀπὸ τοῦ βήματος.
records.gloss: And he drove them from the judgment seat.
pieces: Then he had them driven away from the judgment seat.

L.16: And he drove them from the judgment seat.

R.16: Then he made them leave the court.

decisions.choice: drove away: sent them off, probably by his attendants
decisions.reason: The verb means to drive away. A Roman official had attendants who could clear the place.

decisions.choice: the court
decisions.reason: Readable uses a familiar word for the place where the governor judged cases.

records.source: ἐπιλαβόμενοι δὲ πάντες Σωσθένην τὸν ἀρχισυνάγωγον ἔτυπτον ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ βήματος· καὶ οὐδὲν τούτων τῷ Γαλλίωνι ἔμελεν.
records.gloss: Having seized then all Sosthenes the synagogue ruler they were beating [him] before the judgment seat; and nothing of these things to the Gallio was mattering.
pieces: Then they all grabbed Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, and beat him in front of the judgment seat. But Gallio paid no attention to any of it.

L.17: And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and were beating [him] in front of the judgment seat; and none of these things mattered to Gallio.

R.17: Then they all grabbed Sosthenes, the leader of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the court. But Gallio did not care at all.

decisions.choice: all: probably the crowd of onlookers, Gentiles in Corinth
alternatives: the Jews themselves, angry with their own leader
decisions.reason: Luke does not say who "all" were. Gentile onlookers may have taken Gallio's ruling as leave to attack the Jews' leader. It is also possible that the Jews turned on Sosthenes for losing the case.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "all"
alternatives: a few manuscripts read "all the Jews"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add "the Greeks", and a few add "the Jews". The earliest manuscripts have only "all". Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Sosthenes, the synagogue ruler: perhaps Crispus's successor, or a second ruler
decisions.reason: Some synagogues had more than one ruler (13:15). Paul writes 1 Corinthians with "Sosthenes our brother" (1 Corinthians 1:1). It is not known whether that is the same man.

decisions.choice: none of these things mattered to Gallio: he did not step in
alternatives: he did not know about it
decisions.reason: Gallio let the beating happen in front of his own judgment seat. He had already said these matters were not his concern (18:15).

decisions.choice: in front of the court
decisions.reason: As in 18:16, Readable uses a familiar word.

records.source: Ὁ δὲ Παῦλος ἔτι προσμείνας ἡμέρας ἱκανὰς τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς ἀποταξάμενος ἐξέπλει εἰς τὴν Συρίαν, καὶ σὺν αὐτῷ Πρίσκιλλα καὶ Ἀκύλας, κειράμενος ἐν Κεγχρεαῖς τὴν κεφαλήν, εἶχεν γὰρ εὐχήν.
records.gloss: The now Paul yet having remained days many, to the brothers having taken leave, sailed away to the Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila, having shaved in Cenchreae the head, he had for a vow.
pieces: Paul remained many days longer. Then he took leave of the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} and sailed for Syria, and Priscilla and Aquila went with him. In Cenchreae he had his head shaved, since he had made a vow.

L.18: And Paul, having stayed on many days more, took leave of the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} and sailed away to Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila, having shaved [his] head in Cenchreae, for he had a vow.

R.18: Paul stayed in Corinth for many more days. Then he said goodbye to the believers and got on a ship to go to Syria. Priscilla and Aquila went with him. At the port of Cenchreae he had his hair cut off, because he had made a special promise to God.

decisions.choice: he who shaved his head: probably Paul, possibly Aquila
decisions.reason: The words "having shaved" stand right after Aquila's name, and the form fits either man. But Paul is the subject of the whole sentence, and the story follows him. Later Paul joins men under a vow in Jerusalem (21:23-26).

decisions.choice: a vow: a promise to God, marked by cutting the hair
alternatives: a Nazirite vow ending at the temple, for certain
decisions.reason: Under the Nazirite vow a person let the hair grow and shaved it at the end, at the temple in Jerusalem (Numbers 6:1-21). Shaving the head here, far from the temple, may mark the end of a private vow, or the start of a vow to be completed in Jerusalem. Luke does not say what the vow was for.

decisions.choice: Cenchreae: the eastern port of Corinth
alternatives: a town on the way to Syria
decisions.reason: Cenchreae lay about seven miles east of Corinth on the Saronic Gulf, where ships sailed for Asia and the east. Phoebe served the church there (Romans 16:1).

decisions.choice: Syria: the Roman province, which included Antioch
decisions.reason: Paul's home church was at Antioch in Syria (13:1-3, 14:26). He lands at Caesarea first and comes to Antioch in 18:22.

decisions.choice: Priscilla named before Aquila
decisions.reason: Luke names her first here and in 18:26, as Paul does in Romans 16:3 and 2 Timothy 4:19. This may show that she was the more prominent of the two in the church, but neither writer says why.

decisions.choice: brothers and sisters, with "brothers" as the alternative
decisions.reason: The word means the fellow believers in Corinth, men and women.

decisions.choice: the believers; a special promise to God
decisions.reason: Readable uses plain words for the believers and for a vow.

records.heading: Back to Antioch, and Apollos in Ephesus

records.source: κατήντησαν δὲ εἰς Ἔφεσον, κἀκείνους κατέλιπεν αὐτοῦ, αὐτὸς δὲ εἰσελθὼν εἰς τὴν συναγωγὴν διελέξατο τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις.
records.gloss: They came now to Ephesus, and those he left there, he himself then having entered into the synagogue reasoned with the Jews.
pieces: They arrived at Ephesus, where Paul was to leave Priscilla and Aquila. He went into the synagogue on his own and debated with the Jews.

L.19: And they came to Ephesus, and he left those [two] there, but he himself, having entered into the synagogue, reasoned with the Jews.

R.19: They arrived in the city of Ephesus. Paul left Priscilla and Aquila there. But first Paul went into the synagogue by himself and talked with the Jews about his message.

decisions.choice: Ephesus: the great port city of the province of Asia
decisions.reason: Ephesus lay on the west coast of what is now Turkey, across the Aegean Sea from Corinth. Paul later spends more than two years there (19:8-10).

decisions.choice: he left them there: told first, though it happened after his visit to the synagogue
alternatives: he left them before going to the synagogue
decisions.reason: Luke finishes the couple's part of the story before telling what Paul did. Paul himself leaves Ephesus in 18:21, so his visit to the synagogue came before the parting.

decisions.choice: reasoned: discussed and argued, as in 18:4
decisions.reason: The same verb as in 17:2 and 18:4.

decisions.choice: Priscilla and Aquila
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the two.

decisions.choice: But first; about his message
alternatives: no time word; reasoned with the Jews
decisions.reason: Readable puts the events in order, following the meaning note, and says what the discussion was about.

records.source: ἐρωτώντων δὲ αὐτῶν ἐπὶ πλείονα χρόνον μεῖναι οὐκ ἐπένευσεν, ἀλλὰ ἀποταξάμενος καὶ εἰπών· Πάλιν ἀνακάμψω πρὸς ὑμᾶς τοῦ θεοῦ θέλοντος ἀνήχθη ἀπὸ τῆς Ἐφέσου, καὶ κατελθὼν εἰς Καισάρειαν, ἀναβὰς καὶ ἀσπασάμενος τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, κατέβη εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν, καὶ ποιήσας χρόνον τινὰ ἐξῆλθεν, διερχόμενος καθεξῆς τὴν Γαλατικὴν χώραν καὶ Φρυγίαν, στηρίζων πάντας τοὺς μαθητάς.
records.gloss: Asking now of them for longer time to remain, not he consented, \v 21 but having taken leave and having said, Again I will return to you, the God willing, he sailed from the Ephesus, \v 22 and having come down to Caesarea, having gone up and having greeted the church, he went down to Antioch, \v 23 and having spent time some he went out, passing through in order the Galatian region and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
pieces: They urged him to stay longer, but he would not agree.
As he said goodbye, he told them, "I will come back to you, if God wills," and he put out to sea from Ephesus.
He came ashore at Caesarea, went up to greet the church, and then went down to Antioch.
After some time there he set out again and journeyed through the Galatian country and Phrygia, town after town, building up all the disciples.

L.20: And when they asked [him] to stay for a longer time, he did not consent,
L.21: but taking leave [of them] and saying, "I will return to you again, God willing," he set sail from Ephesus.
L.22: And having landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, [and] went down to Antioch.
L.23: And having spent some time [there], he went out, passing through the Galatian region and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples.

R.20: The Jews there asked Paul to stay longer, but he said no.
R.21: As he was leaving, he told them, "If God wants me to, I will come back to you." Then he sailed away from Ephesus.
R.22: He landed at the city of Caesarea. Then he went up to Jerusalem and greeted the church there. After that he went down to the city of Antioch.
R.23: Paul stayed in Antioch for a while. Then he left and went through the areas of Galatia and Phrygia, visiting one town after another. He helped all the followers of Jesus there to grow stronger.

decisions.choice: they: the Jews of the synagogue in Ephesus
decisions.reason: The last people named are the Jews Paul spoke with (18:19). Their request shows that they were open to hearing more.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: no words about a feast
alternatives: many manuscripts add that he must keep the coming feast in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Codex Bezae and many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add that Paul said he must by all means keep the coming feast in Jerusalem. The earliest manuscripts do not have it. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: God willing: if God allows it
decisions.reason: Paul leaves his plans to God (1 Corinthians 4:19, 16:7; James 4:15). He did come back (19:1).

decisions.choice: he went up and greeted the church: he went up to Jerusalem
alternatives: he greeted the church in Caesarea
decisions.reason: "Going up" is the usual way of speaking of travel to Jerusalem, which stands high in the hills (11:2, 15:2, 21:12). From there one "went down" to Antioch. Luke does not name Jerusalem, so the church could be the one at Caesarea.

decisions.choice: the Galatian region and Phrygia: inland Asia Minor, where Paul had founded churches
alternatives: Galatia far to the north only
decisions.reason: Paul had visited churches in this area before (14:21-23, 16:1-6). Luke names the same areas in the other order in 16:6.

decisions.choice: strengthening: making the believers firm in their faith
decisions.reason: The same verb as in 14:22 and 15:41, where Paul strengthens the churches and urges them to remain in the faith.

decisions.choice: put out to sea
decisions.reason: The verb is a sailing term for setting out from port.

decisions.choice: The Jews there; went up to Jerusalem; stayed in Antioch
alternatives: they; having gone up; having spent some time
decisions.reason: Readable names the people and places, following the meaning notes. Jerusalem is the probable reading, not a certain one.

decisions.choice: the followers of Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable uses the same plain phrase as in 6:1-2.

records.source: Ἰουδαῖος δέ τις Ἀπολλῶς ὀνόματι, Ἀλεξανδρεὺς τῷ γένει, ἀνὴρ λόγιος, κατήντησεν εἰς Ἔφεσον, δυνατὸς ὢν ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς.
records.gloss: A Jew now certain Apollos by name, an Alexandrian by the birth, a man eloquent, came to Ephesus, mighty being in the Scriptures.
pieces: A Jew called Apollos, born in Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was a gifted speaker and could handle the Scriptures with power.

L.24: Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth, an eloquent man, came to Ephesus, being mighty in the Scriptures.

R.24: A Jewish man named Apollos came to Ephesus. He was from the city of Alexandria in Egypt. He was a very good speaker, and he knew the Scriptures very well.

decisions.choice: Alexandria: the great city of Egypt, with a large Jewish community
decisions.reason: Alexandria was a leading center of Greek learning. Many Jews lived there, and the Jewish thinker Philo wrote there in the first century. Jews from Alexandria had their own synagogue in Jerusalem (6:9).

decisions.choice: eloquent: skilled with words, perhaps also learned
decisions.reason: The word can mean a skilled speaker or a man of learning. "Mighty in the Scriptures" already speaks of his learning, so the stress may be on his speaking. Later some in Corinth preferred him to Paul (1 Corinthians 1:12, 3:4-6).

decisions.choice: mighty in the Scriptures: able to explain and argue from the Scriptures
decisions.reason: "Mighty" here means able. 18:28 shows how he used the Scriptures. The Scriptures are what Christians now call the Old Testament.

decisions.choice: the city of Alexandria in Egypt
decisions.reason: Readable says where Alexandria was.

records.source: οὗτος ἦν κατηχημένος τὴν ὁδὸν τοῦ κυρίου, καὶ ζέων τῷ πνεύματι ἐλάλει καὶ ἐδίδασκεν ἀκριβῶς τὰ περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, ἐπιστάμενος μόνον τὸ βάπτισμα Ἰωάννου.
records.gloss: This [man] was having been instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in the spirit he was speaking and was teaching accurately the things concerning the Jesus, knowing only the baptism of John.
pieces: He had been taught the way of the Lord, and with great zeal he spoke and taught the facts about Jesus correctly, though the only baptism he knew was John's.

L.25: This [man] had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in spirit, he was speaking and teaching accurately the things concerning Jesus, knowing only the baptism of John.

R.25: Someone had taught him about the way of the Lord. He was full of excitement when he spoke and taught, and what he taught about Jesus was correct. But the only baptism he knew about was the one John had preached.

decisions.choice: the way of the Lord: the teaching about how God saves and how his people should live
decisions.reason: "Way" is used of a manner of life and of teaching (13:10, 18:26). Later Luke calls the movement of believers "the Way" (19:9, 19:23). "Instructed" is the word used for teaching new believers (Luke 1:4).

decisions.choice: fervent in spirit: full of zeal in his own spirit
decisions.reason: The verb means to boil. Paul uses the same words in Romans 12:11 for zeal. Some take "spirit" to mean the Holy Spirit, but Apollos knew only John's baptism, and the phrase reads more naturally of his own eagerness.

decisions.choice: accurately: correctly, though not completely
decisions.reason: The word means exactly or carefully. What he taught was right; 18:26 says Priscilla and Aquila explained the way "more accurately", adding to it rather than correcting errors.

decisions.choice: knowing only the baptism of John: he knew John's baptism of repentance, but not baptism in the name of Jesus
alternatives: he had not been baptized at all
decisions.reason: John baptized people who repented, to prepare them for the one coming after him (13:24-25; 19:4). The followers of John in 19:1-7 had not heard of the Holy Spirit. Luke does not say whether Apollos was baptized again.

decisions.choice: the Greek order, close to other literal versions
decisions.reason: Literal follows the Greek wording here, so it will look like other word-for-word translations.

decisions.choice: the one John had preached
decisions.reason: Readable says what John's baptism was: the baptism John called people to receive.

records.source: οὗτός τε ἤρξατο παρρησιάζεσθαι ἐν τῇ συναγωγῇ· ἀκούσαντες δὲ αὐτοῦ Πρίσκιλλα καὶ Ἀκύλας προσελάβοντο αὐτὸν καὶ ἀκριβέστερον αὐτῷ ἐξέθεντο τὴν ὁδὸν τοῦ θεοῦ.
records.gloss: He then began to speak boldly in the synagogue. Having heard however him, Priscilla and Aquila took him and more accurately to him expounded the way of the God.
pieces: He started to speak out fearlessly in the synagogue. Priscilla and Aquila heard him there, and they took him in and taught him the way of God more precisely.

L.26: And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him [to themselves] and expounded to him the way of God more accurately.

R.26: Apollos began to speak boldly in the synagogue. Priscilla and Aquila heard him. So they took him to their home and helped him understand God's way more fully.

decisions.choice: to speak boldly: to speak openly and without fear
decisions.reason: The same word is used of the apostles and of Paul (4:13, 4:31, 9:27-28, 13:46).

decisions.choice: took him: took him aside, probably into their home
decisions.reason: The verb means to take someone to oneself, to welcome. They did not correct him in public.

decisions.choice: more accurately: filling out what he already knew
decisions.reason: The word picks up "accurately" in 18:25. They added what he lacked, such as baptism in the name of Jesus.

decisions.choice: Priscilla named first, and she shares in teaching Apollos
decisions.reason: Both are the subject of the verb "expounded". As in 18:18, she is named first.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "Priscilla and Aquila"
alternatives: many later manuscripts read "Aquila and Priscilla"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, put Aquila first. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: took him to their home
decisions.reason: Readable follows the meaning note, which is likely but not certain.

records.source: βουλομένου δὲ αὐτοῦ διελθεῖν εἰς τὴν Ἀχαΐαν προτρεψάμενοι οἱ ἀδελφοὶ ἔγραψαν τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἀποδέξασθαι αὐτόν· ὃς παραγενόμενος συνεβάλετο πολὺ τοῖς πεπιστευκόσιν διὰ τῆς χάριτος·
records.gloss: Wishing then he to pass through into the Achaia, having encouraged [him] the brothers wrote to the disciples to welcome him, who having arrived helped much those having believed through the grace;
pieces: Apollos planned to go across to Achaia, and the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} encouraged him in it. They wrote to the disciples there, asking them to welcome him. Once he came, he gave much help to those who had come to believe through grace,

L.27: And when he wanted to go across to Achaia, the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, encouraging [him], wrote to the disciples to welcome him; and when he arrived, he greatly helped those who had believed through grace,

R.27: Apollos wanted to go to the province of Achaia. The believers in Ephesus encouraged him to go. They wrote a letter to the followers of Jesus in Achaia and asked them to welcome Apollos. When he got there, he was a great help to the people who had believed through God's grace.

decisions.choice: through grace: they believed by God's grace
alternatives: he helped them by God's grace
decisions.reason: The phrase can go with "believed" or with "helped". Next to "believed" it says that their faith was God's gift (15:11); with "helped" it says that Apollos's help came from God's grace (compare 14:26, 15:40).

decisions.choice: encouraging him: they urged Apollos on
alternatives: they urged the disciples in Achaia to welcome him
decisions.reason: The participle has no object. It may mean that the believers in Ephesus backed Apollos's plan, or that their letter urged the disciples to receive him.

decisions.choice: Achaia, and a letter of recommendation
decisions.reason: Achaia was the province whose chief city was Corinth; Apollos is there in 19:1. Believers wrote letters to introduce one another to other churches (Romans 16:1-2; 2 Corinthians 3:1).

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: the shorter text
alternatives: Codex Bezae says Corinthians in Ephesus invited him to their city
decisions.reason: Codex Bezae and some other Western witnesses rewrite the verse: some Corinthians staying in Ephesus urge Apollos to come to their home city, and he agrees. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: those who had believed: the believers in Corinth
decisions.reason: Paul writes that he planted and Apollos watered (1 Corinthians 3:6).

decisions.choice: brothers and sisters, with "brothers" as the alternative
decisions.reason: The believers in Ephesus, men and women.

decisions.choice: the believers in Ephesus; the followers of Jesus in Achaia
decisions.reason: Readable names the groups in plain words and says where each was.

records.source: εὐτόνως γὰρ τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις διακατηλέγχετο δημοσίᾳ ἐπιδεικνὺς διὰ τῶν γραφῶν εἶναι τὸν χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν.
records.gloss: vigorously for the Jews he was refuting publicly, showing through the Scriptures to be the Christ Jesus.
pieces: for he argued powerfully and publicly against the Jews, proving them wrong, and used the Scriptures to show that Jesus is the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

L.28: for he was vigorously refuting the Jews in public, showing through the Scriptures that the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} was Jesus.

R.28: He argued strongly with the Jews in front of everyone, and he proved that they were wrong. He used the Scriptures to show that Jesus is the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: for: this explains how he helped the believers
decisions.reason: His public debates with the Jews of Corinth supported the believers there (18:27).

decisions.choice: was refuting: proving them wrong, thoroughly
decisions.reason: The verb is strong: to refute completely. The tense shows he did this again and again.

decisions.choice: the Christ was Jesus: the promised Messiah is Jesus
decisions.reason: The same words as in 18:5. Apollos made the same case Paul had made, from the same Scriptures.

decisions.choice: that Jesus is the Messiah (with Christ as the setting)
decisions.reason: As in 18:5, Literal keeps the Greek order; Balanced and Readable use the order English readers expect.

decisions.choice: a new sentence
decisions.reason: Readable starts a new sentence, so the link word is left out.
